assumption: Years after the cross are counted from AD 30 (if the crucifixion was AD 33, subtract 3).

cards.name: Flavius Josephus (Testimonium Flavianum)
cards.quote: Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man
cards.quote_note: Opening words only. The full passage in Whiston's English translation, including lines most scholars think a Christian copyist added, is in the Library file.
cards.shows: A Jewish historian writing about 60 years after the cross mentions Jesus as a teacher and wonder-worker who had followers among Jews and Gentiles and was condemned to the cross by Pilate.
cards.does_not_prove: It does not prove the resurrection. Lines like 'He was [the] Christ' and 'he appeared to them alive again the third day' are widely judged to be later Christian additions, so we do not lean on them.
cards.scholarly_status: Majority view: Josephus wrote a shorter, neutral passage about Jesus that a Christian copyist later expanded. A 10th-century Arabic summary by Agapius gives a more cautious wording that many see as support for an authentic core. T. C. Schmidt (Oxford University Press, 2025) (Josephus and Jesus: New Evidence for the One Called Christ) argues that the whole passage is substantially Josephus' own; that is a minority but serious view.
cards.confidence_note: Core mention: widely accepted. Full wording: contested.

cards.name: Flavius Josephus (James, brother of Jesus)
cards.quote: the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James
cards.shows: In passing, Josephus identifies James by his famous brother, 'Jesus, who was called Christ', and records James' execution by the high priest Ananus around AD 62.
cards.does_not_prove: It says nothing about Jesus' teaching, miracles or resurrection. It shows that Jesus was a known, real person.
cards.scholarly_status: Widely accepted as authentic by most scholars, Christian and non-Christian. A few argue 'who was called Christ' is a later note.

cards.name: Tacitus
cards.stance: Roman senator and historian, hostile to Christians
cards.quote: Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilatus
cards.translator: John Jackson, Loeb Classical Library (1937), via LacusCurtius
cards.shows: A top Roman historian, who despised Christians, confirms that Christ was executed under Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius, that the movement spread to Rome, and that Nero punished Christians after the fire of AD 64.
cards.does_not_prove: Tacitus does not say where he got his information, and he says nothing about the resurrection. He calls the faith a 'pernicious superstition'.
cards.scholarly_status: Accepted as genuine by nearly all historians. Pilate was technically a prefect (the Pilate stone says praefectus); Tacitus uses the title of his own day.

cards.name: Pliny the Younger, with Emperor Trajan's reply
cards.work: Letters 10.96 (X.97 in the Melmoth/Bosanquet numbering), reply 10.97 (X.98)
cards.quote: addressed a form of prayer to Christ, as to a divinity
cards.translator: William Melmoth, revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet
cards.shows: A Roman governor in what is now Turkey reports that Christians met before dawn on a fixed day, worshipped Christ as divine, and promised not to steal, cheat or commit adultery. Some were executed for refusing to deny Christ. This shows Jesus was worshipped as God long before Constantine.
cards.does_not_prove: Pliny describes what Christians believed and did in his day, not the events of Jesus' life.
cards.note_for_site: Other translations render this line as 'a hymn to Christ as to a god'. Quote the Melmoth wording exactly when using this card.

cards.name: Suetonius (Claudius)
cards.quote: Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome.
cards.translator: J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library (1914), via LacusCurtius
cards.shows: Probably a garbled reference to disputes over Christ among Jews in Rome, about AD 49. This fits Acts 18:2, where Aquila and Priscilla have left Rome because Claudius expelled the Jews.
cards.does_not_prove: 'Chrestus' was also an ordinary name, and Suetonius seems to think the man was in Rome. It is not a clear reference to Jesus.
cards.scholarly_status: Debated. Many scholars think Chrestus means Christ; others think it was a local agitator.

bible_link.text: There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to visit them,

cards.name: Suetonius (Nero)
cards.quote: Punishment was inflicted on the Christians, a class of men given to a new and mischievous superstition.
cards.translator: J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library (1914), via LacusCurtius
cards.shows: Confirms, independently of Tacitus, that Nero punished Christians in Rome in the 60s.

cards.name: Lucian of Samosata
cards.quote: The Christians, you know, worship a man to this day,--the distinguished personage who introduced their novel rites, and was crucified on that account.
cards.translator: H. W. Fowler and F. G. Fowler, The Works of Lucian of Samosata vol. IV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1905)
cards.shows: Even a mocker takes for granted that Christians worshipped a man who was crucified, and describes how they cared for each other and did not fear death.
cards.does_not_prove: Lucian is late and is mocking; he is a witness to what Christians believed in his day.

cards.name: Celsus (as quoted by Origen)
cards.work: The True Word (lost), quoted in Origen, Against Celsus 1.32 and Book 2
cards.date_written: Celsus about AD 175-180; Origen's reply about AD 248
cards.quote: although he somehow granted that Jesus worked miracles, he thought to weaken the force of this by the charge of sorcery
cards.quote_note: These are Origen's words describing Celsus.
cards.shows: The earliest known written attack on Christianity never denies Jesus existed or was crucified. It explains his miracles as sorcery, which means even critics accepted that unusual deeds were reported.
cards.does_not_prove: Celsus' charges are hostile, and we only have them through Origen.
cards.scholarly_status: Accepted that Origen quotes Celsus at length and fairly closely.
cards.framing: Celsus repeats a slander that Jesus was the son of a soldier named Panthera (Origen 1.32). Present this gently: it is an attack on the virgin birth, and it shows that even opponents knew Jesus' birth was unusual. Origen answers it directly.

cards.name: Thallus and Phlegon (as quoted by Julius Africanus)
cards.work: Quoted in Julius Africanus, Chronography fragment XVIII
cards.date_written: Thallus uncertain (possibly 1st century); Phlegon about AD 140; Africanus about AD 221
cards.quote: This darkness Thallus, in the third book of his History, calls, as appears to me without reason, an eclipse of the sun.
cards.shows: If Africanus is reporting correctly, a pagan writer was already trying to explain away the darkness at the crucifixion as an eclipse.
cards.does_not_prove: Thallus' own words are lost, and we cannot be sure he mentioned Jesus by name. Thallus' date is debated. Phlegon's eclipse may be a different event.
cards.scholarly_status: Debated. Treat as a supporting clue, not a pillar.

cards.name: Mara bar Serapion
cards.date_written: debated: some time after AD 73, possibly much later
cards.quote: Or the Jews by the murder of their Wise King, seeing that from that very time their kingdom was driven away from them?
cards.translator: B. P. Pratten, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8 (1886)
cards.shows: A non-Christian writer compares the killing of a Jewish 'Wise King' to the deaths of Socrates and Pythagoras, and says he lived on through 'the new laws which he enacted'.
cards.does_not_prove: He never names Jesus, and the date of the letter is uncertain.
cards.scholarly_status: Many think the Wise King is Jesus; others are cautious. Date debated.
cards.framing: Mara is a pagan writer reflecting on ancient events. This is not a statement about Jewish people then or now, and the Gospels place the execution in Roman hands.

cards.name: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 43a
cards.stance: Jewish rabbinic tradition, critical of Jesus
cards.date_written: Talmud compiled about AD 500; the tradition is older, date debated
cards.paraphrase: In our own words: an older tradition quoted in the Talmud says that on the eve of Passover, Jesus of Nazareth (Yeshu ha-Notzri) was executed and his body hung up. For forty days beforehand, it says, a herald announced that he would be stoned for sorcery and for leading Israel astray, and invited anyone to speak in his defense, but no one was found.
cards.shows: Even a hostile Jewish tradition assumes Jesus of Nazareth was real and was executed on the eve of Passover, and explains his deeds as sorcery rather than denying them. The Passover-eve timing fits John 19:14.
cards.does_not_prove: The written form is late, and it describes stoning, not crucifixion, so it is not an independent eyewitness record. The forty-day herald is not in any Christian account and is usually seen as a later defensive claim.
cards.scholarly_status: Most scholars think this Yeshu refers to Jesus; some see it as a reaction to Christian claims rather than independent memory.
cards.framing: For a church audience: this is an opponent's account, given here so people are not caught off guard. Read it with respect for the Jewish community today; it reflects ancient debates.
cards.license_note: Checked the Sefaria page via its API on 26 Oct 2026: the English William Davidson Edition is CC BY-NC. We paraphrase and link, and do not reproduce its text.
cards.confidence_note: That the passage exists and says this: Confirmed. What it tells us historically: Contested.

bible_link.text: It was the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour. And Pilate said to the Jews, “Here is your King!”
